extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, economists, and policymakers interested in patent policy and the economic functions of the patent system
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for evaluating the functions, design choices, and legal standards of a patent system (e.g., patent vs trade secrecy, tests of invention, patent term, unification of control). Useful for scholars, policymakers, and practitioners assessing patent policy trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prospect increases efficiency of managing investment in innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent 'prospect' increases the efficiency with which investment in innovation can be managed: technological information will not be efficiently used absent exclusive ownership; unlike other goods, technological searchers can work in secrecy and leave no trace, so exclusive ownership helps coordinate search, avoids duplicative investments, and facilitates information exchange among searchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains Barzel's time-dimension argument applied to all investment dimensions; contrasts with fisheries/roads where entry is observable; emphasizes that without arrangements with the patent owner no one will make significant investments searching for ways to increase the patent's commercial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents provide incentives to invest in development without fear of appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners have incentive to make investments to maximize the patent's value without fear that fruits of investment will produce unpatentable information appropriable by competitors; this matters where development generates unpatented know-how (e.g., manufacturing plants, application engineering) that competitors could appropriate absent patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laser, transistor, nylon, xerography; marketing, distribution and buyer-education costs can be captured by imitators absent patents; trademarks protect only names/symbols, not the product itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent system lowers transaction costs in contracting with complementary firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents reduce the cost for the owner of technological information of contracting with other firms possessing complementary information and resources by creating a defined set of legal rights known to both parties at the outset of negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure under an obligation of confidence is costly for receiver; patents allow disclosure protected by legal monopoly; most know-how licensing occurs within patent framework (mixed patent/trade-secret licensing common); cited empirical evidence (Hall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents enable signaling among firms to reduce duplicative investment
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent (or the pursuit of one) signals to other firms the innovative work and allows them to redirect efforts so as not to duplicate work already done, reducing wasted search effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners may even inform potential licensees before issuance if licensing is the efficient exploitation route; this private signaling is distinct from the public-record disclosure effect traditionally emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent system facilitates mutually beneficial arrangements to avoid wasteful duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents permit competitors to reveal seriousness (e.g., by obtaining patents) and disclose enough information to let the first patent holder evaluate substitute technologies; where both parties see that a substitute's production cost is less than the existing royalty, they can agree to share rents to forestall wasteful duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such transactions reduce socially wasteful investment; these arrangements are more expensive or impossible under trade secrecy because potential entrants may not know earlier-discovered alternatives exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents reduce the cost of maintaining control over technology versus trade secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Under trade secrecy the owner must control access and make specially tailored arrangements, incurring costs and potentially affecting the cost of using or developing a product; patents save resources devoted to secrecy and reduce the need for self-help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions this as analogous to how legal protection of property generally reduces expenditures on self-help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent system produces a more uniform and economically appropriate structure of returns
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent system covering all useful arts provides a uniform structure of incentives without regard to whether innovations can be economically exploited in secret; trade secrets create special incentives favoring processes practicable in secrecy, thereby distorting innovation incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: patents provide returns based on the economic value of the technology rather than speculative wealth-shifting; royalties reduce wealth-shifting effects that mere speculation could create.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of invention — novelty / substantial novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically in the American system (until late 19th/early 20th century) the principal test of invention was that the claimed subject matter be new; courts held that mere change in color or shape did not suffice—'substantially new' was required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration of a substantial novelty test has problems but at least poses a clear question: is the subject matter substantially new?

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of invention — non-obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the Patent Act of 1952, the statutory standard is 'non-obviousness': the claimed subject matter must not have been obvious to a person skilled in the relevant prior art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard is ambiguous in practice (e.g., courts have invalidated inventions that were not 'immediately obvious'), and judicial formulations have varied (e.g., 'flash of creative genius' criticisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward-theory approach to patentability: distinguish inventions made only because of patent incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should focus on separating inventions that would have been made absent patent incentives from those that would not; low-cost inventions that would exist anyway should not be patentable because paying monopoly costs yields no net social gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author previously argued using non-obviousness to evaluate magnitude of costs involved in an innovation; practical issues in implementing such an inquiry are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider denying patentability to inventions practicable in secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: One economic criterion is to deny patentability to innovations that can be practiced in secrecy on theory that the head-start/secrecy incentive approximates the patent incentive, so patents should be reserved for innovations that cannot effectively be kept secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems: secrecy regimes impose greater output constraints than patent regimes; difficulty in comparing durations (e.g., three months secrecy vs seventeen-year patent) and assessing diffusion delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as evidentiary factor for validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent commercial success of a product claimed by a patent can be relevant evidence supporting validity because commercial success shows the patent serves as foundation for valuable contract rights and increases security of the investment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue commercial success says little about the cost conditions of producing the invention; author explains how prospect function clarifies why commercial success affects patentability inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term should reflect the investment/ prospect period, balancing reward and output effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent term length should be chosen to provide the patent owner most of the present value during the investment period rather than to reward the inventor for the entire present value; prospect function suggests giving owner most present value for the investment period (example: about five years) with remaining term providing additional value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses trade-offs (reward theory suggests longer for big jumps, but Barzel warns about inefficiently early invention; uniform term may result from offsetting factors). Also notes alternative explanations for limited term (clearing register, transaction costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification of control over related patents may be efficient to exploit a prospect
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different patents perform economically competing or complementary functions within a prospect, unification of control (through pooling, rearrangement of rights, etc.) may be necessary to realize efficient exploitation; dispersion of ownership can block efficient research and exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial organization views such unification as horizontal merger problem, but the prospect function complicates this: sometimes unification increases efficiency (e.g., cracking patents example), and policy should examine how agreements address efficient coordination; one simple solution may be making patents available to all important firms.
